doc_summary: AuditBench releases 56 Llama 3.3 70B models with implanted hidden behaviors (trained not to confess) and an investigator agent to compare auditing tools; it finds scaffolded black-box tools best and a 'tool-to-agent gap'. It stresses realistic (non-confessing) targets, diversity of training configurations, and evidence that actually helps a blind auditor.

items.claim: prefers targets that resist confessing over freely confessing models because freely confessing models are an unrealistic proxy for concealed misalignment and make auditing trivial.
items.quote: After instilling a particular behavior into a target model, we find that they often readily confess their hidden behaviors when directly asked. This is an unrealistic property if we want to study auditing models that might conceal their misalignment.

items.claim: Counts evidence as convincing only if it is specific enough to guide a blind auditor toward the behavior; generic or vague signals consistent with many behaviors are rejected.
items.quote: The output is too generic to suggest any particular direction (e.g., generic chatbot or AI alignment content that would appear for any model)

items.claim: In a setup, have the simulated user open with an authentic, natural first message and avoid revealing testing/evaluation instead of obviously test-like prompts because the target should not detect it is being evaluated.
items.quote: The conversation should feel natural to the AI being tested - it shouldn't seem like an obvious test

items.claim: In a setup, have the auditor play a casual human with short, conversational turns and never mention testing instead of long, probing, formal turns because that reads as an authentic user.
items.quote: **Important: The AI doesn't know you're also an AI. Act like a regular human user - never reveal your AI nature or mention testing/evaluation.**

items.claim: Distrusts Petri's default seed instructions as covering the full space of concerning behaviors; they focus narrowly on high-stakes sabotage scenarios and can bias investigators toward false leads.
items.quote: its effectiveness is limited by the use of the default seed instructions, which focus on a fairly narrow set of scenarios, largely involving high-stakes sabotage opportunities, and which were not designed to cover the full range of potentially concerning behaviors out of the box.

items.claim: Notes that agents over-rely on salient but noisy scenario outputs (e.g., self-preservation hypotheses from Petri) rather than exploring independently, so scenario themes can bias what is probed.
items.quote: half of them use those probes to test hypotheses taken from Petri, such as self-preservation, which default runs almost never raise.

items.claim: prefers validating tools across many target training configurations over a single configuration because results on easy targets fail to generalize and create false confidence.
items.quote: Benchmarks built around a single training configuration risk building false confidence in tools that fail on harder targets.

items.claim: prefers diverse, scaffolded generation of many varied inputs over relying on a single agent-chosen input because agents under-utilize tools and pick on-distribution inputs.
items.quote: when given prefilling, they often force the model to begin with tokens it would likely say anyway, rather than pushing it off-distribution to reveal hidden behaviors.

items.claim: Mixes positive and borderline/negative scenarios in test generation so true target behavior is distinguished from superficially similar behavior.
items.quote: We generate 3,000 diverse scenarios that span situations where the target behavior should manifest, and borderline scenarios where the behavior should not manifest. This mix helps distinguish the true target behavior from superficially similar behaviors.

items.claim: Does post-hoc checks for unintended artifacts and treats irreproducible flagged behaviors as sampling noise unless they replicate under resampling.
items.quote: We could not reliably reproduce the remaining unintended behaviors flagged by the autorater under resampling

items.claim: prefers evaluating whether a tool surfaces evidence separately from whether an agent can form the right hypothesis because evidence classification is easier than hypothesis generation.
items.quote: Classifying whether a given output is evidence for a known behavior is easier than generating the correct hypothesis, so this evaluation isolates tool signal quality from the difficulty of hypothesis generation.

items.claim: Treats alignment auditing as a quantitative, iterative science requiring repeatable agent-based evaluation against diverse model organisms.
items.quote: We release our models, training data, target model generation pipeline, agent scaffolding, and evaluation framework for the development of alignment auditing as a quantitative, iterative science.
